subject: Computing

unit.unitTitle: Devices That Talk to Each Other
unit.unitOverview: First, that many different devices can connect to a network — not only computers, but also things like a smart TV, a smart light bulb, an e-reader, a scanner and a security camera. Second, that two devices can work together, and that a device joined to others can do much more than a device standing all alone. Third, you learn to say the words wired (joined with a cable you can see) and wireless (joined through the air, with no cable), and to tell the two apart. Almost everything here is unplugged — done on paper, with string and cards, or by acting things out — so no hardware is needed. Keep every explanation short, use real objects and actions, and you can talk and move. Letting you act as devices, joined by string and passing a message hand to hand, teaches the idea better than any screen could.

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Computing 0672 — Stage 2 Teacher & Parent Guide, Activity Sheet and Mini-Project. Teacher-directed prose was rewritten into learner-facing explainers so the unit teaches with no adult present.

outcomes: Know that many different devices can connect to a network — not just computers, but also a smart TV, a smart bulb, an e-reader, a scanner and a security camera.
Say what a network is — devices joined together so they can share and send messages.
Understand that two devices can work together, and that a joined (connected) device can do more than a device on its own (standalone).
Know that connected devices can share things like a printer, and share files such as photos.
Explain the words wired (joined with a cable) and wireless (joined through the air, no cable), and tell them apart.

concepts.title: Devices that can join a network
concepts.explanation: A device is a machine like a tablet, a phone or a printer. When we join devices together so they can share and send messages, we make a network. Lots of devices — not only computers — can join a network. You already know that tablets, laptops and phones can join a network. But guess what — many more devices can join too!
concepts.example: Start with what you know. Keep each to one friendly sentence.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you understand that some everyday things (a pencil, a book) cannot join a network? Can you name two or three devices that can join a network beyond a plain computer?

concepts.title: Alone or joined? (working together)
concepts.explanation: A device on its own is a standalone device. It cannot talk to any other device. When we join a device to others, it becomes a connected device — and two connected devices can do more together than one device can do alone. Imagine you are all alone in a room with the door shut. You cannot pass a note to a friend, because there is no friend to pass it to. That is a standalone device — all by itself. Now open the door and join hands with a friend.
concepts.example: Now you can pass notes, share your toys, work together. That is a connected device.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you name one thing connected devices can share, like a printer or a photo? Can you tell the difference between a standalone device (alone, cannot share) and a connected device (joined, can share)?

concepts.title: Wireless networks (no wires!)
concepts.explanation: A wireless network joins devices through the air, with no cable at all. Because there is no wire holding them, the devices can move around and still stay joined. Wireless networks are popular in homes and cafes. Tablets, laptops and phones usually join wireless networks. When you carry a tablet from the kitchen to the garden and it still works, that is a wireless network. There is no cable trailing behind you — the network reaches you through the air, a bit like sound or sunshine. That is why you can walk about and stay joined.
concepts.example: Find one real example of wireless networks (no wires!) around you, or on a device you use. Say out loud what it is and why it fits.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you know that wireless devices can move around and stay joined?

concepts.title: Wired networks, and telling them apart
concepts.explanation:
A wired network uses cables to join devices. You can see the wire. Because a cable holds a device in place, wired devices do not move around. Wired networks are often used in schools and offices. A good example of a wired device is a desktop computer, which sits still on a desk.

A wired network has cables, like this. You can see them.
concepts.example: A desktop computer stays on its desk, joined by a cable — it does not walk around. Wired networks are strong and steady, so schools and offices like to use them.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you match a moving device to wireless and a still device to wired?

concepts.title: Draw and sort our networks
concepts.explanation: This session pulls the unit together. There is nothing new to learn — it is a happy chance to use every word from the unit: device, network, connect, share, wired, wireless. Today you are the network builders! You will draw devices, join them together, and say whether your network is wired or wireless.
concepts.example: Do it yourself: draw and sort our networks. Work through it slowly, then check what you did against the explanation above.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you draw a small network with at least three labelled devices, joined together?

esafety.title: Keep personal information private
esafety.text: Your full name, address, school, phone number, birthday and passwords are personal information. Never type them into a game, an app or a website, and never send them to someone you only know online.

esafety.title: Check before you trust
esafety.text: Anyone can put anything on the internet, so not everything you read is true. Check an important fact on a second, different website, and ask an adult you trust if you are not sure.

esafety.title: Tell someone if something worries you
esafety.text: If anything online upsets you, or someone asks you for personal information or to keep a secret, stop, leave the page and tell an adult you trust straight away. It is never your fault.

esafety.title: Respect other people's work
esafety.text: Pictures, music and writing belong to whoever made them. Use work that is free to use, and say where you got it. Your own work belongs to you — put your name on it.

A device on its own can share with others.
A standalone device is all alone; it cannot share or talk to other devices. It must be connected first.
Wireless devices cannot move / wired devices can move.
It is the other way round. Wireless devices can move around and stay joined; wired devices are held in place by their cable.
If we share one printer, everyone still needs their own.
No — the whole point of a network is that many devices can share one printer.

project.brief: Bring together everything from Devices That Talk to Each Other into one finished piece of work you can show and explain.
steps: Plan first: write down what your devices that talk to each other project has to do before you build anything.
Build the smallest version that does one of those things, and run it.
Add one feature at a time, testing after each one.
When something breaks, change one thing, run it again, and note what fixed it.
Check your work against every success criterion below before you call it finished.
successCriteria: I drew at least three devices and labelled them.
I joined my devices together (with lines or a Wi-Fi box).
I said if my network is wired or wireless.
I wrote one thing my devices can do together.

selfAssessment: I can know that many different devices can connect to a network — not just computers, but also a smart TV, a smart bulb, an e-reader, a scanner and a security camera.
I can say what a network is — devices joined together so they can share and send messages.
I can understand that two devices can work together, and that a joined (connected) device can do more than a device on its own (standalone).
I can know that connected devices can share things like a printer, and share files such as photos.
I can explain the words wired (joined with a cable) and wireless (joined through the air, no cable), and tell them apart.
